title: CP template — fast I/O, macros & type aliases

hook.scenario: You start a competitive programming contest. You spend the first 3 minutes typing `#include <iostream>`, `#include <vector>`, `using namespace std;`, and setting up `cin.tie(NULL)`. You've already lost time compared to higher-ranked competitors.
hook.question: How do Grandmasters avoid writing the same 20 lines of boilerplate every single match?

mental_model.intuition: A CP template is like a chef's 'mise en place'. Before the cooking timer even starts, all the ingredients (tools, aliases, optimizations) are already chopped, measured, and placed exactly where you need them.
mental_model.description: A CP (Competitive Programming) template is a standardized header block that you copy-paste at the start of every contest. It includes universal headers (like `<bits/stdc++.h>`), type aliases (like `using ll = long long;`), and standard fast I/O boilerplate to ensure your program reads input optimally without manual setup.

explanation:
**1. The Master Header:**
Instead of `#include <iostream>`, `#include <vector>`, etc., competitors use `#include <bits/stdc++.h>`. This is a non-standard GCC header that includes *every* standard library header at once. It slows down compilation slightly, but saves immense typing time during contests.

**2. Fast I/O Setup:**
By default, `std::cin` and `std::cout` are tied to C's `stdio` (printf/scanf) to allow mixing C and C++ I/O. This synchronization makes C++ I/O incredibly slow. `ios_base::sync_with_stdio(false);` unties C++ streams from C's `stdio`, making C++ streams vastly faster. However, because they now have independent buffering, mixing `cin`/`cout` with `scanf`/`printf` leads to unpredictable, interleaved output. `cin.tie(NULL);` does something entirely different: it unties `cin` from `cout`, preventing `cout` from automatically forcing an expensive buffer flush every time input is read.

**3. Type Aliases & Macros:**
`long long` is verbose. `using ll = long long;` saves typing. 
Macros like `#define pb push_back` or `#define all(x) (x).begin(), (x).end()` are extremely common to compress algorithms into fewer keystrokes.

**Real-world Engineering vs. CP:**
While a CP template is essential for racing against a 2-hour clock, it is considered **terrible practice in production engineering**. `#include <bits/stdc++.h>` ruins build times and isn't portable. `#define` macros pollute the global namespace and make debugging impossible. Keep these tricks strictly for contests.

common_mistakes.title: Using std::endl instead of "\n"
common_mistakes.explanation: `std::endl` doesn't just output a newline; it also flushes the output buffer. Flushing the buffer is an expensive OS-level operation. In problems with massive output, flushing on every line will cause a Time Limit Exceeded (TLE) error. Always use `"\n"` in CP.

recall_questions.answer: It disables the synchronization between C++ streams (`cin`/`cout`) and C streams (`scanf`/`printf`), which significantly speeds up C++ I/O. However, it means you can no longer safely mix C and C++ I/O functions.

recall_questions.q: Why is `#include <bits/stdc++.h>` used in CP but banned in production?
recall_questions.answer: It includes the entire standard library at once, saving typing time in contests. In production, it severely inflates compilation times and is a compiler-specific hack (GCC) rather than a C++ standard.

recall_questions.q: Why should you avoid `std::endl` in competitive programming?
recall_questions.answer: `std::endl` automatically flushes the output stream. Frequent flushing causes massive I/O latency and often leads to Time Limit Exceeded (TLE). You should use the newline character `"\n"` instead.

oa_questions.question: A competitor includes the fast I/O lines in `main()`, but their program crashes or outputs garbage data because they used both `cin >> x` and `scanf("%d", &y)` sequentially. Why did this happen?
oa_questions.answer: Because `ios_base::sync_with_stdio(false)` unties the internal buffering of C and C++ I/O streams. Mixing them after untying results in unpredictable interleaving of reads and writes.
oa_questions.approach: Understand the side-effects of performance hacks.

oa_questions.question: A developer submits a solution with `std::cout << ans << std::endl;` inside a loop running 10^6 times. They get TLE. They change it to `std::cout << ans << "\n";` and pass. Why did this fix it?
oa_questions.answer: `std::endl` forces a buffer flush to the operating system on every single iteration. `"\n"` simply adds a newline character to the buffer, allowing the stream to write to the OS in large, efficient chunks.
oa_questions.approach: Identify I/O bottlenecks in tight loops.

key_points.title: Fast I/O is mandatory
key_points.detail: Always disable sync with stdio and untie `cin` from `cout`.

key_points.title: Never flush in a loop
key_points.detail: Use `"\n"` instead of `endl` to prevent I/O bottlenecks.

why_it_exists: In Competitive Programming, you are graded against a strict time limit (usually 1-2 seconds). Reading 1 million integers using standard synchronized `std::cin` can easily take 0.8 seconds, leaving almost no CPU time for your actual algorithm. CP templates exist to instantly inject I/O optimizations and shorthand aliases so you can focus entirely on the logic without hitting artificial timeouts.
